topic: Permanent and induced magnetism, magnetic forces and fields
subject: physics

items.q: The north pole of one bar magnet is brought close to the north pole of a second bar magnet. What happens to the magnets?
items.correct: They repel each other, because the two poles are alike
items.misconception: They attract, because magnets always pull each other
items.why: Nearly every everyday encounter with a magnet is an attraction - fridge magnets, magnetic catches, picking up paper clips. Repulsion only shows up when a student deliberately turns one magnet round. Whether the force is a push or a pull depends only on which poles face each other. Like poles (N-N or S-S) repel; unlike poles (N-S) attract. Both are equally ordinary magnetic behaviour.
items.random_wrong: Nothing happens until the two magnets are touching

items.q: Two magnets on a bench push each other apart while there is still a 2 cm gap between them. Which statement best describes this force?
items.correct: It is a non-contact force, acting across the air gap
items.misconception: It is a contact force passed through the bench surface
items.why: Most forces a student meets - pushing a trolley, friction, tension - do need contact, so contact feels like a requirement for any force. Attraction and repulsion between two magnetic poles are examples of non-contact force. The force is felt through the gap and gets stronger as the gap closes.
items.random_wrong: It is a non-contact force only while they move

items.q: A steel paper clip is held near a strong magnet and becomes magnetic itself. What name is given to the paper clip while it is in the field?
items.correct: The clip is an induced magnet
items.misconception: The clip is a permanent magnet
items.why: A chain of paper clips hanging from a magnet looks permanent while the magnet is there, and steel objects can retain a little magnetism, which seems to confirm it. Induced magnetism depends on the field being present. Take the field away and the induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly, so the chain falls apart.
items.random_wrong: The clip is a non-magnetic metal

items.q: A chain of paper clips hangs from a bar magnet. The magnet is taken away. What happens to the paper clips?
items.correct: They lose their magnetism and fall apart
items.misconception: They stay in a chain, now permanently magnetic
items.why: A chain of paper clips hanging from a magnet looks permanent while the magnet is there, and steel objects can retain a little magnetism, which seems to confirm it. Induced magnetism depends on the field being present. Take the field away and the induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly, so the chain falls apart.
items.random_wrong: They push each other apart and scatter widely

items.q: The south pole of one bar magnet is brought near the north pole of another. Which row correctly describes the force?
items.correct: Attraction, because unlike poles attract each other
items.misconception: Repulsion, because these two poles are different
items.why: The rule is a pair of near-identical sentences that differ by one word, so it is easy to memorise them the wrong way round, and everyday language says like things go together. Two like poles repel each other. Two unlike poles attract each other. Testing it with two bar magnets, N facing N gives a push and N facing S gives a pull.
items.random_wrong: Attraction, because south poles always attract

items.q: A student wants two magnets on trolleys to push apart when released. How should the magnets be arranged?
items.correct: With two north poles facing each other
items.misconception: With a north pole facing a south pole
items.why: The rule is a pair of near-identical sentences that differ by one word, so it is easy to memorise them the wrong way round, and everyday language says like things go together. Two like poles repel each other. Two unlike poles attract each other. Testing it with two bar magnets, N facing N gives a push and N facing S gives a pull.
items.random_wrong: With the two magnets touching end to end

items.q: Which statement gives a correct difference between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet?
items.correct: A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field
items.misconception: An induced magnet keeps its magnetism when it is removed
items.why: A chain of paper clips hanging from a magnet looks permanent while the magnet is there, and steel objects can retain a little magnetism, which seems to confirm it. Induced magnetism depends on the field being present. Take the field away and the induced magnet loses most or all of its magnetism quickly, so the chain falls apart.
items.random_wrong: A permanent magnet can only ever attract things

items.q: An iron nail is brought near the south pole of a magnet and is pulled in. The magnet is then turned round so the north pole faces the nail. What happens?
items.correct: The nail is still pulled towards the magnet
items.misconception: The nail is pushed away, as the pole has changed
items.why: Students transfer the like-poles-repel rule from two permanent magnets to a case where only one of the objects is a permanent magnet. The poles induced in the material always line up so that the nearer induced pole is unlike the pole causing it. The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction.
items.random_wrong: The nail is pushed away only when it is close

items.q: Which of these is the best definition of a magnetic field?
items.correct: The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet
items.misconception: The area a magnet covers when it is touching an object
items.why: Most forces a student meets - pushing a trolley, friction, tension - do need contact, so contact feels like a requirement for any force. Attraction and repulsion between two magnetic poles are examples of non-contact force. The force is felt through the gap and gets stronger as the gap closes.
items.random_wrong: The set of lines drawn on a diagram around a bar magnet

items.q: A magnet is held over a tray containing a copper coin, a nickel disc, an aluminium strip and a steel screw. Which objects are attracted?
items.correct: Only the nickel disc and the steel screw
items.misconception: All four of them, since they are all metals
items.why: The magnetic objects a student meets at home - tins, screws, fridge doors - are almost all steel, so metal and magnetic look like the same category. Copper, aluminium, brass, gold and tin are metals but are not magnetic materials. The specification names iron, steel, cobalt and nickel as the magnetic materials.
items.random_wrong: The copper coin and the steel screw

items.q: A bar magnet is brought near an unmagnetised iron bar. The magnet is then flipped end for end. Which statement about the force on the iron bar is correct?
items.correct: It stays an attraction, whichever pole faces the bar
items.misconception: It now changes from an attraction to a strong repulsion
items.why: Students transfer the like-poles-repel rule from two permanent magnets to a case where only one of the objects is a permanent magnet. The poles induced in the material always line up so that the nearer induced pole is unlike the pole causing it. The force between a magnet and a magnetic material is always one of attraction.
items.random_wrong: It becomes zero, because the two poles now cancel out

items.q: Where is the magnetic field of a bar magnet strongest?
items.correct: At the poles of the magnet
items.misconception: In the middle of the magnet
items.why: Students reason by bulk - more metal in the middle should mean more magnetism - and iron filings pictures are often cropped so the ends are cut off. The poles of a magnet are the places where the magnetic forces are strongest. Iron filings cluster at the ends of a bar magnet and barely gather at its middle.
items.random_wrong: Equally strong at every point

items.q: A plotting compass is moved slowly away from the north pole of a bar magnet. What happens to the magnetic field where the compass is?
items.correct: It gets weaker, because the distance from the magnet increases
items.misconception: It stays exactly the same until a definite edge is reached
items.why: Diagrams show a finite number of field lines ending at the edge of the page, which reads as a boundary where the field switches off. The field is strongest at the poles and gets steadily weaker with distance from the magnet. It fades away rather than ending at a sharp edge.
items.random_wrong: It gets stronger as the compass moves away from the pole

items.q: Outside a bar magnet, which way do the magnetic field lines point?
items.correct: From the north pole to the south pole
items.misconception: From the south pole across to the north
items.why: The needle's north end points along the field, but students remember the needle as being pulled to the magnet's north pole and reverse the arrows. Outside the magnet the arrows go N to S. The direction of the field at any point is the direction of the force on another north pole placed there.
items.random_wrong: From each pole in towards the middle

items.q: A compass is placed at a point in the field of a bar magnet. What does the direction the needle's north end points in tell you?
items.correct: The direction of the magnetic field at that point
items.misconception: The straight line from that point to the nearest pole
items.why: Near a pole the needle really does aim close to it, and students generalise that one case to every position around the magnet. The needle takes the direction of the field where it stands. Along the side of a bar magnet that direction is roughly parallel to the magnet, not aimed at a pole.
items.random_wrong: The direction the compass would travel if released

items.q: What is inside a magnetic compass?
items.correct: A small bar magnet
items.misconception: A light piece of iron
items.why: The needle looks like a plain sliver of metal, and students know that magnets attract iron, so attraction seems enough to explain it. A magnetic compass contains a small bar magnet. Only a magnet has poles that can be pushed one way and pulled the other, which is what turns the needle to a definite direction.
items.random_wrong: A coil of thin wire

items.q: A compass is placed on a bench with no magnets anywhere near it. What does the needle do?
items.correct: It settles pointing along the Earth's own magnetic field
items.misconception: It keeps spinning slowly, as there is no field present
items.why: Students associate a field only with a nearby bar magnet, so with no magnet on the bench there seems to be nothing for the needle to respond to. The Earth has a magnetic field of its own. With no other magnet near, the needle lines up with that field, which is why a compass works out of doors.
items.random_wrong: It points towards the coldest part of the whole room

items.q: A student is plotting the field pattern of a bar magnet using a plotting compass. Which method is correct?
items.correct: Mark a dot at each end of the needle, then move the compass on
items.misconception: Slide the compass all the way round the magnet while touching it
items.why: Most forces a student meets - pushing a trolley, friction, tension - do need contact, so contact feels like a requirement for any force. Attraction and repulsion between two magnetic poles are examples of non-contact force. The force is felt through the gap and gets stronger as the gap closes.
items.random_wrong: Draw a straight line from the compass to the nearest pole

items.q: A student draws the field pattern of a bar magnet. Which feature of the drawing shows that the field is stronger near the poles?
items.correct: The lines are drawn closer together there
items.misconception: The lines are drawn a long way apart there
items.why: The word spread gets attached to strength, and the long lines that stretch furthest from the magnet look like the important ones. The spacing of the lines shows strength: crowded lines near the poles show the strongest field, and widely spaced lines at the sides show a weaker field.
items.random_wrong: The lines are drawn with two arrows on them

items.q: A compass points the same way on a bench, in a field and out at sea, with no magnets nearby. What does this suggest about the Earth?
items.correct: The core of the Earth must be magnetic
items.misconception: The ice at the North Pole acts like a magnet
items.why: Students look for a visible cause at the surface, and the polar ice cap is the most obvious feature at the top of a globe. A compass points the same way anywhere, with no magnet present, so the field must come from the Earth itself. This is evidence that the core of the Earth must be magnetic.
items.random_wrong: The atmosphere is what pulls the needle

items.q: Is a magnetic field only there when something is in it?
items.correct: No. A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field whether or not anything else is nearby.
items.misconception: The field only appears when a piece of iron or another magnet is brought close.
items.why: You can only detect a field by its effect on something, so the effect and the field get treated as the same thing. The magnetic field is the region around the magnet where a force would act. It is there all the time; a compass or a piece of iron reveals it rather than creating it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does a compass needle point north?
items.correct: Because it lines up with the direction of the Earth's magnetic field.
items.misconception: It is pulled towards the North Pole because that is the coldest and highest point on the map.
items.why: North on a map is drawn at the top, and the North Pole is a single named place, so the needle looks like it is aiming at a location rather than along a field. The needle is a small bar magnet lining up with the Earth's magnetic field at that point. It reports a field direction, not the position of a place.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can the north pole of a magnet attract another magnet?
items.correct: Yes, if it is facing the south pole of that magnet.
items.misconception: A single pole by itself fixes the force: a pole is treated as 'an attracting pole' or 'a repelling pole', instead of the force depending on which two poles face each other.
items.why: Students attach attract and repel to a single pole rather than to the pair of poles facing each other. No pole attracts or repels on its own. It is the combination that matters: like poles repel, unlike poles attract.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a compass need a current or a coil to work?
items.correct: No. A magnetic compass contains a small bar magnet and needs no electrical parts.
items.misconception: The needle is turned by a coil of wire inside the case, like an electrical instrument.
items.why: Compasses look like meters, and students meet coils and needles together when they later study electromagnetism, so the two get merged. A magnetic compass contains a small bar magnet, free to turn. It has no battery, coil or current; the needle turns because it is itself a magnet sitting in a magnetic field.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Paper clips hang in a chain from a magnet. If the magnet is taken away, will the clips push each other apart?
items.correct: No. The clips were only induced magnets; when the magnet is removed they lose their induced magnetism and simply fall apart.
items.misconception: The magnet gives every clip the same magnetism, and things carrying the same magnetism push each other apart, like two objects with the same electric charge.
items.why: Magnetism is blended with static electricity: students learn that objects charged by contact carry like charges and repel, and transfer that rule to paper clips 'magnetised' by touching the magnet. Magnetism is not a charge that is shared out. Each clip becomes an induced magnet whose facing poles are opposite, which is why the chain attracts and holds together. When the magnet is removed the induced magnetism largely disappears, so the clips just fall apart - they do not repel each other.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Will a copper coin be attracted to a magnet?
items.correct: No. Copper is not a magnetic material; only iron, steel, cobalt and nickel are attracted to magnets.
items.misconception: Copper is magnetic, because 'copper' coins stick to a magnet at home.
items.why: UK 1p and 2p coins made since 1992 are steel with a thin copper plating, so they really do stick to a magnet; the everyday result is credited to the copper on the outside, while nickel is not recognised as magnetic at all. The magnetic materials are iron, steel, cobalt and nickel. Pure copper is never attracted to a magnet. Modern 'copper' coins stick only because of the steel underneath the copper coating.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A magnet is brought near an unmagnetised iron bar. Which pole appears on the end of the bar nearest the magnet?
items.correct: The opposite pole to the one facing it, so the induced magnet is always attracted to the magnet.
items.misconception: The magnet prints its own pole onto the iron: the end of the bar nearest a north pole becomes a north pole, so the magnet and the bar repel.
items.why: Induced magnetism is pictured as the magnet copying or stamping its magnetism onto the iron, so the near end is given the same pole as the pole that 'made' it, which would put like poles face to face. Induction always produces the opposite pole on the near end of the iron: a north pole induces a south pole facing it, and a south pole induces a north pole. That is why induced magnetism always causes attraction, whichever pole of the magnet is used.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.7.1 Permanent and induced magnetism, magnetic forces and fields
